stories.headline: OpenAI ships GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol, claiming the top score on Agents' Last Exam at a fraction of Fable 5.2's cost
stories.why_read: The biggest model launch of the week and the top story on Hacker News with more than 800 comments, and it reprices the frontier you build agents on.
body: OpenAI released GPT-6.2 Astra, its new frontier model for the hardest projects, and GPT-6.2 Sol, an efficient model for everyday work. Both are pitched on doing more with fewer output tokens. On Agents' Last Exam, a benchmark of long-horizon professional workflows, OpenAI says Astra scores 5.2 points above GPT-6 Astra at less than a third of the cost, and 5.5 points ahead of Claude Fable 5.2 at about 5% of the cost. It also claims new highs on Terminal-Bench-Science 0.1, 9 points above GPT-6 Astra, and on the Vals Science Index, and calls Astra the best model in the world for scientists.

API pricing for Astra drops 20% from GPT-6 Astra: $8 per million input tokens, $0.40 cached and $40 output. Sol keeps GPT-6.1 Sol's prices while getting smarter and more efficient, and OpenAI says many of its employees use it as their default. Note the footnote: Agents' Last Exam leaderboard results for Fable 5.2 exclude nine tasks that fell back to another model.

stories.headline: Tesla unveils Powercore, its first solid-state transformer, built for fully off-grid data centers
stories.why_read: You bookmarked both posts: Tesla Energy moving from batteries into grid hardware, aimed squarely at the AI data-center power crunch.
body: Tesla Megapack introduced Powercore, a solid-state medium-voltage transformer, inverter and breaker in one unit. Tesla rates it at 7.4 MW / 9 MVA continuously at 34.5 kVac, with grid-forming support for 10 MVA of peak power. It is made in America and is due to begin operating in 2027.

Sawyer Merritt's summary adds a peak efficiency of 98.86% and frames the pitch: paired with Megapacks, Powercore is meant to let data centers run fully off-grid. Transformers have been one of the longest-lead items in the power build-out, so a Tesla-built solid-state option matters as much for supply as for specs.

stories.headline: Java4Shell: a bug in OpenJDK's AVX-512 Base64 decoder gives pre-auth RCE in Keycloak, Jira, Confluence, Jenkins and more
stories.why_read: Rated 9.2 critical and sitting under almost every enterprise Java stack you run; this is a patch-today story for an IT architect.
body: Calif disclosed CVE-2026-114938, a memory-corruption bug in hand-written assembly that OpenJDK uses to speed up Base64 decoding with AVX-512 VBMI instructions on x86-64. A short crafted input, 64 'A' characters and one '=' (128 on OpenJDK 17), makes the decoder write 64 bytes past the end of its output buffer. Calif turned that into heap reads in the style of Heartbleed and remote code execution.

In default configurations they demonstrated pre-auth RCE in Keycloak, Atlassian Jira and Confluence, JFrog Artifactory, Jenkins and PingFederate, and post-auth RCE in Kafka, Solr, Elasticsearch, Gerrit and Spinnaker. Temurin, Microsoft, Azul, Liberica, SapMachine, Red Hat and Oracle builds are all listed as affected. Because the bug only fires on CPUs with those instructions, exposure depends on your hardware, and the authors close with a call to strip out code you do not need.

stories.headline: Banks and the NSA tell Congress this week's outages came from rushing to patch flaws that AI models found, as the NSA's own classified network goes dark
stories.why_read: You retweeted it: the first credible explanation for a week of strange failures, and a warning about what AI-scale vulnerability discovery does to change control.
body: The Washington Sun's Jeff Stein reports, citing three sources, that Wall Street executives and the NSA told lawmakers this week's widespread tech failures were caused by attempts to fix vulnerabilities identified by AI. AI did not cause the outages, the sources say, but found so many issues that the rush to patch them before attackers could act overwhelmed systems.

Separately, CNN reports that the highly classified network the NSA uses for internal communications is down, according to six people familiar with the matter, and that the agency closed its campus to most employees on Tuesday night while it works on a restore. CNN does not give a cause. Either way, it is a case study in why patch velocity needs the same staging and rollback discipline as feature work.

stories.headline: Tesla Robotaxi in Miami's expanded geofence: zero issues through construction zones, and $10.11 against Waymo's $17.80
stories.why_read: You retweeted it: a rider's report from a new market, with a price comparison that shows where the robotaxi fight is heading.
body: Ray4Tesla took several Tesla Robotaxi rides in the expanded Miami service area, through construction zones and a range of urban situations, and reports zero issues, calling the trips exceptionally smooth and saying human-driven taxis are "not even on the same level".

The number to remember is the fare: his comparison shows Tesla charging $10.11 for a trip that cost $17.80 on Waymo, nearly 43% less. Tesla's Eric E. added his own note on Cybercab's design goal, a ride meant to feel indistinguishable from your favorite comfortable chair at home.

stories.headline: SpaceX wins a Texas air permit to build its own 31 MW gas power plant at Starbase, off the public grid
stories.why_read: You retweeted it: SpaceX quietly joins the behind-the-meter power trend, right as Tesla pitches off-grid power hardware.
body: Texas regulator TCEQ approved the project at SpaceX's Starbase production site on November 16, according to Muskonomy. The plan calls for three natural gas turbines generating 31.14 MW combined, with all of the electricity used on site.

The turbines include controls to reduce nitrogen oxide and carbon monoxide emissions, and the permit lets SpaceX power Starbase without relying on the public grid, a useful hedge for a factory that is ramping Starship production.

stories.headline: Microsoft's MAI Code 2 claims 96% of Opus 5.5's coding performance at 5% of the cost
stories.why_read: Microsoft now has its own coding models aimed at GitHub Copilot-style everyday work, and the price-performance claims are aggressive.
body: Microsoft AI announced MAI Code 2 and MAI Code 2 Flash at Ignite, two coding models built for everyday enterprise tasks. Averaged across DeepSWE 1.1, Terminal Bench 2.1, SWE-Atlas and FrontierCode v1.1, Microsoft says MAI Code 2 delivers 98% of GPT-6.1 Sol's performance at 40% of the cost and 96% of Claude Opus 5.5's at just 5%. In blind frontend evaluations, reviewers preferred its results over GPT-6 Sol 64% of the time.

Flash targets high-volume work such as explanations, targeted edits and routine fixes, and Microsoft says it matches GPT-6 Luna and Claude Haiku 5.5 on three routine-coding benchmarks at a fraction of their cost. Microsoft is upfront that the models are not yet tuned for fundamental research or very long-horizon agentic work.

stories.headline: Five Grok Bots now hold full-time jobs on SpaceXSI's accounting team, each owning one order-to-cash process end to end
stories.why_read: A concrete blueprint for scoping bots to one job each and only pulling in humans for judgment, which is exactly how your own fleet is set up.
body: In a post on x.ai, the SpaceXSI accounting team describes five Team Bots, each with a carefully scoped responsibility. Provisioning Bot checks contracts and opens or closes customer accounts. Billing Bot checks that billing data matches the executed contract before it generates and sends invoices. Billing Support Bot handles requests from the go-to-market team. Cash Applications Bot applies payments, investigates discrepancies and flags short payments. Collections Bot handles billing inquiries and refunds.

The team says the bots are onboarded, trained and managed like human teammates, and involve a person only when the work needs judgment or approval. The result, they write, is handling more work without growing headcount at the same rate.

stories.headline: A car-dealer YouTuber spends a full day being driven by a Tesla: "I don't think the auto industry fully understands what's coming"
stories.why_read: You bookmarked and retweeted it: an industry insider, not a Tesla fan, reacting to current FSD.
body: The Guy Dealership, who covers the car business, posted an eight-minute video of a day spent being driven by a Tesla, with the verdict that the auto industry does not grasp what is coming.

The X news summary of the discussion around it points to FSD Supervised 14.3.13, with smoother handling around emergency vehicles and in low visibility and five driving profiles from Chill to Mad Max. Owners in the replies share near-flawless experiences, while the debate continues over how far supervised driving is from true autonomy.

stories.headline: Uber is undercutting Tesla's Cybercab in Austin, with UberX rides showing as low as $4.95
stories.why_read: Your city is the first real price war between human-driven rideshare and robotaxis.
body: Abhimanyu Yadav posted screenshots showing Uber prices in Austin lower than what Tesla charged before Cybercab launched, and asked how Uber can make money, or what the driver gets, on trips like these. He also notes Tesla fixed a navigation issue he had flagged, which brought its own price for the trip down.

The X news roundup of the thread puts the comparison at $4.95 for an UberX with an 8-minute wait, against $7.55 for a Cybercab arriving in 2 minutes or $7.27 for a Model Y robotaxi in 10. Some riders say they pick the robotaxi for speed even when it costs more.

stories.headline: Life after Jensen: the board wants a new culture, Bezos says hire from within, and Nvidia is now spending more cash than it makes
stories.why_read: You retweeted half a dozen takes last night; here they are in one place, plus the FT on Nvidia's Singapore disclosure.
body: Gene Munster says Jensen Huang's Nvidia chapter is over and the board is signaling it wants a new culture. Jay Yarow's take is blunter: Huang thought export chip controls were dumb and acted as if he were above the law. Jeff Bezos, in a clip shared by Stock MKT News, said that if Huang does not return, Nvidia should pick its next CEO from inside the company.

On the numbers, Stock Savvy Shay points out that Nvidia's cash fell sequentially for the first time in four years because it spent $22B on buybacks and $6B on dividends, deploying more than it generates. Apollo CEO Marc Rowan told CNBC that Nvidia has been "the bank or the guarantor of the AI ecosystem". And per a Financial Times story on the Hacker News front page, Nvidia stopped disclosing Singapore sales as revenue hit $104B.

stories.headline: Anthropic may price its IPO above $80 a share on strong demand, valuing it around $1.5 trillion
stories.why_read: You bookmarked Ferragu's framing of the deal; here is the latest pricing news behind it.
body: Per the Wall Street Journal, as relayed by The Kobeissi Letter, Anthropic is weighing a higher IPO price after stronger-than-expected investor demand, possibly above $80 a share against an initial range of $70 to $78. Advisers have discussed a valuation of about $1.5 trillion to $1.6 trillion, up from roughly $1.33 trillion at the original range.

Pierre Ferragu, whose post you bookmarked, shared a chart offering "a very simple way to think about Anthropic's IPO". The X news roundup also notes a reported $10 billion purchase by Nvidia as part of a $26 billion private placement.

stories.headline: Brad Gerstner: only 26% of Anthropic's compute this year served paying customers, and the rest went mostly to training
stories.why_read: A counterintuitive read on inference economics: serving is a smaller cost than the scale of the build-out suggests.
body: Speaking about Anthropic, Altimeter's Brad Gerstner said the company had about two gigawatts of compute this year and only about a quarter of it, roughly 500 megawatts, went to serving customers. He ties that slice to about $100 billion in revenue.

His conclusion is that if the consensus forecast of another $100 billion in revenue next year holds, serving it needs far less new capacity than the headlines imply, because training is where most of the compute goes. The X news summary cites Anthropic's S-1 as putting training at 74% of compute.

stories.headline: A next-amino-acid test suggests the latest Claude models were trained on protein sequences at scale, and Fable 5.2 beats open protein LMs
stories.why_read: A clever black-box probe that reveals what is in a frontier model's training data; no other model, GPT-6.2 included, shows the effect.
body: Xinming Tu gave models the start of little-studied bacterial proteins and asked for the next amino acid. Claude Fable 5.2 and Opus 5.5 predict it; on shuffled proteins they cannot, and no other frontier model tested shows the effect. Like a protein language model, Claude does better on bigger protein families, even in families with no papers about them.

Fable 5.2 beats every open protein language model the author ran, including ProGen3-3B, and Opus 5.5 is level with ProtGPT3-10B. An 18 November update adds 56 proteins first made public in August 2026, which the latest Claude models still predict, and confirms GPT-6.2 Sol and Astra show no sign of it.

stories.headline: Cerebras puts GPUs on prefill and wafer-scale engines on decode, claiming 5x more tokens per megawatt
stories.why_read: Disaggregated prefill/decode is the inference architecture trend of the year, and this is the first heterogeneous version in production.
body: Cerebras says it is now running disaggregated inference in production: GPUs handle prompt processing (prefill) and Cerebras systems handle output generation (decode). The company claims five times more tokens per megawatt at its usual ultrafast speeds.

It will use the setup to grow its own inference cloud and offer it to infrastructure partners for their data centers. Cerebras pairs the news with its CS-4 system, scaled-up manufacturing and 700 MW of planned data-center capacity.

stories.headline: SGLang hits v1.0 and launches a consortium with Nvidia, AMD, Intel, Google, Meta and Cloudflare as founding members
stories.why_read: The open-source inference engine behind production serving at Meta is now a cross-vendor standard effort.
body: At the first SGLang Summit, with more than 2,000 attendees over two days, the project announced SGLang v1.0, released Miles v0.2 and launched the SGLang Consortium. The nine founding members are Nvidia, AMD, Intel, Google, Meta, Thinking Machines, Cloudflare, Modal and RadixArk.

SGLang says it is used by 332 organizations, and at Meta it powers production inference for products serving billions of users. Teams from Modal, Cloudflare and LinkedIn shared production lessons across 90+ talks and six workshops on inference, reinforcement learning and agents.

stories.headline: Energy-Based Reasoners: a 1.8M-parameter looped model hits 99.9% on Sudoku-Extreme with 345x less inference compute
stories.why_read: A physics-flavored idea for reasoning models, with a built-in verifier and a natural stopping rule.
body: Researchers from Duke, UIUC and Harvard propose Energy-Based Reasoners, looped reasoning models that learn an energy function over latent reasoning states and treat each loop as gradient descent on that energy. The energy scores candidate answers without an external verifier, and its gradient both refines the answer and signals when to stop.

With only 1.8M parameters, they report 99.9% accuracy on Sudoku-Extreme using 345 times less inference compute than the next-best model, plus state-of-the-art coverage on N-Queens and graph coloring with near-100% single-sample accuracy.

stories.headline: FrontierHarness Eval v1.1: across 22 coding harnesses and 5 models, the best harness changes with the model
stories.why_read: If you swap models in your agent stack, this says you should probably swap the harness too.
body: Runta and Baseten ran 22 harnesses against 5 models on 62 tasks with 4 attempts each, 83B tokens over 27,280 agent runs. Each model had a different best-value harness: Codex CLI with GLM-5.3, Pi with GLM-5.3 Flash, ZCode with DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, Oh My Pi with Muse and Alma with Kimi-K3.

Cost rankings swung widely: by cost per task the median harness moved 11 of 22 places, and Codex CLI went from 1st with GLM-5.3 to 16th with Kimi-K3. Across all models, OpenCode v2 had the lowest cost per task at $0.561 and ZCode the highest pass rate at 61.9%.

stories.headline: Harvard study of 718 firms: AI coding agents added about 30% more code, but review took 49% longer and finished work didn't rise
stories.why_read: Hard data behind yesterday's verification theme: the bottleneck moved from writing code to reviewing it.
body: In a working paper covering 718 firms, Harvard Ph.D. candidates Fiona Chen and James Stratton found that engineers at companies adopting AI coding agents added about 30% more code, yet finished work did not measurably rise and getting code through review took 49% longer.
It is a job-market paper with no indication of completed peer review, but the measurement idea travels: track approved work, revision rates and reviewer time, not just drafting output.

stories.headline: Why Gemini 4 Carbon is so slow: about seven times the steps and sixteen times the input tokens of GPT-6 Astra
stories.why_read: A clean trace-level teardown of agent latency that applies to any model you are evaluating.
body: Kernel noticed Gemini 4 Carbon spent close to an hour on tasks that Opus and Astra finished in minutes, echoing complaints from Theo and others. Tracing every step, they found the model simply does more work per task.

Compared with GPT-6 Astra, Carbon takes about seven times as many steps and eleven times as many actions such as reading files or running commands, writes about seven times as much, and because every step re-sends a growing conversation, processes more than sixteen times as much input.

stories.headline: Mark Gurman: two months after Siri AI, Apple has been "completely jettisoned yet again" by Meta and Google
stories.why_read: You bookmarked and retweeted it: Apple's most-followed reporter says Apple has fallen behind in consumer AI again.
body: Bloomberg's Mark Gurman says that two months after launching Siri AI, Apple has again been left behind in the space, and that the "real" AI for consumers is now coming not just from the labs but from Apple's two biggest competitors, Meta and Google.
It is a sharp turn from the Siri AI launch narrative, and it lands the same week OpenAI, Microsoft and Google all pushed new models.

stories.headline: Dario Amodei warns that uncontrolled open-model releases could lead somewhere "very dangerous", and open-source advocates push back
stories.why_read: The open-weights debate you follow, in Anthropic's CEO's own words, right as Databricks shows open models taking enterprise share.
body: In a clip shared widely on X, Amodei argues that a company deploying its own model can monitor usage, revoke a user's access and change what the model will do, while a model released in an uncontrolled way leaves all of that "entirely out of your hands". He says advocates should be challenged to solve that problem.
Critics in the thread compare the stance to rejecting Linux and read it as a push for corporate control of intelligence; supporters point to misuse risks such as biological threats.

stories.headline: The Trump administration has weighed requiring US companies to disclose on their websites when they use Chinese AI models
stories.why_read: If it happens, it touches any stack quietly running Qwen or DeepSeek, which is a lot of them.
body: Walter Bloomberg relayed a report that the administration has mulled requiring US companies to disclose their use of Chinese AI models on their websites.

The X news summary says Treasury and White House officials discussed the idea, aimed at slowing adoption through public awareness and market pressure rather than a ban, and notes models like Alibaba's Qwen and DeepSeek already power parts of customer service at companies such as DoorDash and Airbnb.

stories.headline: Genesis AI raises a $500M Series A at $3.5B to build general-purpose robots with human-level dexterity
stories.why_read: One of the largest robotics Series A rounds yet, backed by Nvidia's and AMD's venture arms.
body: Co-founder Zhou Xian announced the round, saying Genesis is building general-purpose robots that work reliably across whole workflows for years, to remove the physical limits on human ambition.

The X news summary says the Paris-based startup's backers include Nvidia and AMD venture arms, Khosla Ventures and Eric Schmidt, and that it trains its GENE model with sensor gloves that capture human hand motion.

stories.headline: A randomized experiment finds Google's AI Overviews cut clicks to websites by about 40%
stories.why_read: Unusually rigorous evidence on what AI answers do to the open web, and the GEO industry has no fix yet.
body: Revscope reports a randomized experiment in which researchers hid AI Overviews from some US desktop users. Compared with users who still saw them, an Overview cuts clicks to outside websites by about 40%. Overviews now appear on more than half the US keywords DataForSEO tracks, up from 6% two years ago.
Generative engine optimization has not shown a way to make up the loss: in March, AI assistants sent websites just 0.3% of their traffic.

stories.headline: Cloudflare calls Quad9's withdrawal from France a canary in the coal mine for DNS-level blocking
stories.why_read: A free, privacy-focused DNS resolver exiting a whole country over court-ordered blocking is a real infrastructure precedent.
body: Quad9, the Swiss non-profit, said last month it will pull its free public DNS resolver out of France after a court imposed daily penalties for not blocking domains tied to alleged copyright infringement.

Cloudflare's Patrick Nemeroff and Christiaan Smits argue the ruling left Quad9 choosing between crippling penalties and undermining its users' privacy and security. They warn that demanding blocking at every layer of the Internet will drive basic infrastructure services away.

stories.headline: Tailscale's guide to a self-hosted FreshRSS feed for blogs, YouTube and release notes, read from anywhere on your tailnet
stories.why_read: You retweeted it: a weekend-sized homelab project that gets your reading out of algorithmic feeds.
body: Tailscale's Kevin walks through setting up FreshRSS to pull favorite blogs, YouTube channels and software updates into one chronological feed, then reading it from a phone or laptop over Tailscale without exposing the server to the internet.

stories.headline: Casey Handmer had AI audit his entire PhD field: 158,059 papers, and an estimate that peer review catches about one error in five
stories.why_read: A striking use of AI as a literature auditor, with numbers on how long errors keep getting copied.
body: Handmer screened every paper with full text in his former field, recomputed and checked 659 of the most important, and followed every verified error through the papers that cite it. Among revised papers, 13 verified errors were fixed between preprint and journal version while 56 went through review into print, which he reads as peer review removing about one error in five.

Errors persist: the share of copied errors still being copied is 52% at year 7 and 39% at year 10. Extrapolating from the papers checked so far, he estimates about 34,000 undetected errors (25,000 to 48,000) in the field's papers cited 100 or more times.

stories.headline: 350 years ago this month, Ole Rømer predicted a late eclipse of Io and proved light has a finite speed
stories.why_read: A short, satisfying history of one of physics' great predictions, on its anniversary.
body: In September 1676 the Danish astronomer told the Académie des Sciences in Paris that on November 9, Jupiter's moon Io would emerge from the planet's shadow about ten minutes later than expected. He was right. The delay came from the extra distance light had to travel as Earth moved away from Jupiter.

Rømer concluded light took about 22 minutes to cross the diameter of Earth's orbit, which works out to roughly 225,000 km/s against today's value of about 300,000 km/s. Huygens and later Newton backed the idea fairly quickly.

stories.headline: Nike accepts a Mississippi senator-elect's challenge to give every valedictorian custom Air Force 1s, and takes it nationwide
stories.why_read: You retweeted it: a small, generous gesture that went bigger than anyone asked.
body: Senator-elect Scott Colom challenged Nike to give every high school valedictorian in Mississippi a pair of custom Air Force 1s. Nike accepted, and says it will expand the incentive nationwide.
As Yashar Ali notes, it will cost Nike no more than a few million dollars and generate many times that in goodwill.
